subsystems.name: Protein feedstock
subsystems.role: provides the structural proteins that give the printed material its strength and function.
parts: recombinant structural proteins (e.g., silk, collagen, elastin)

subsystems.name: DNA origami scaffold
subsystems.role: programmable DNA nanostructures that position proteins with nanometre precision.

subsystems.name: Bioink
subsystems.role: printable formulation carrying proteins and scaffolds.

subsystems.name: Printing hardware
subsystems.role: deposits the bioink layer by layer at high resolution.

subsystems.name: Folding and crosslinking
subsystems.role: locks the printed proteins into their functional shape.

subsystems.name: Characterisation and integration
subsystems.role: verifies structure and adds living cells or actuators.

buildSteps.title: Design the protein and its DNA template
buildSteps.detail: Choose a structural protein sequence and design DNA origami staples that will bind and align it; simulate folding and assembly.

buildSteps.title: Produce the protein
buildSteps.detail: Insert the gene into bacteria, yeast or mammalian cells, grow them in bioreactors, then harvest and purify the protein.

buildSteps.title: Formulate the bioink
buildSteps.detail: Mix purified protein with crosslinkers and other additives to reach the right viscosity and printability.

buildSteps.title: Print the structure
buildSteps.detail: Use a 3D printer to deposit the bioink layer by layer, optionally co-printing DNA origami scaffolds and living cells.

buildSteps.title: Trigger folding and crosslinking
buildSteps.detail: Change temperature, pH or light to fold the proteins and lock the structure; DNA origami may self-assemble into programmed patterns.

buildSteps.title: Post-process
buildSteps.detail: Wash away unreacted components, dry or hydrate the construct, and add coatings or cells.

buildSteps.title: Test and iterate
buildSteps.detail: Measure stiffness, strength and elasticity; image the nanoscale ordering; refine design and printing parameters.

prerequisites.why: some structural proteins like spider silk are made in pilot plants, but yields and cost need improvement.
nanoscale DNA shapes are routinely made in labs, but scaling to macroscale structures is hard.
extrusion and light-based printers can deposit cells and hydrogels, but protein structural materials are less developed.
folding is understood, but controlling it inside a printed object remains difficult.
enzymatic and photo-crosslinking are used in tissue engineering, but need tuning for structural proteins.

pathway.milestone: lab demonstrations of 3D-printed protein hydrogels and DNA origami templating
pathway.unlocks: proof that proteins can be patterned at small scale.

pathway.milestone: printed protein composites with mechanical properties approaching natural materials
pathway.unlocks: bio-mimetic materials for implants or soft robotics.

pathway.milestone: integration of living cells and contractile proteins for synthetic muscle
commercial-scale production of printed protein structures
